narrative:
The model has analyzed your academic situation and determined that there’s a **22% chance** you might not pass your final year. While this isn’t a certainty, it’s high enough that your school has decided you should take extra remedial courses to help you succeed. Think of it like a warning sign—your current path has some risks, and these courses are a way to give you the support you need to stay on track.

The decision wasn’t made randomly—it was based on three key factors that stood out in your profile. The first is your **study habits**. Right now, you’re studying between **2 to 5 hours a week**, which is less than most students who are doing well. While you haven’t failed any classes yet, this lower study time is a red flag, especially since many students who pass spend more time preparing.

The second factor is your **aspirations for the future**. You’ve said you want to pursue higher education, which is great! But the model noticed that students who are serious about their long-term goals often put in extra effort now. Since you’re not currently studying as much as others with similar ambitions, there’s a risk you might struggle to keep up.

Finally, your **family and home environment** play a role. While you have a supportive family—your mother is your guardian, and you receive family help with school—your parents’ education levels are lower than average for students who succeed. This doesn’t mean you can’t do well, but it suggests you might need extra guidance to bridge any gaps in academic support at home.

The good news is that these courses aren’t a punishment—they’re a chance to strengthen your weak spots. Focus on increasing your study time, especially in areas where you’re falling behind, and take advantage of any extra help your family or school can offer. Small changes now can make a big difference in your final results.

The target variable is whether the student will fail their final year.

Protected attributes sex, age and health were not used to make the machine prediction.
